AAA: The safest slices of collateralized loan obligations, bundles of corporate loans where this fund's top-rated tranches get paid first. It pays more interest than Treasury bonds with very high credit quality, though CLOs are complex and their prices can drop when loan markets panic.
AAPR: America's largest companies with a defined shield stretched over two years, ending in April 2028: it is designed to protect against losses across the whole period, in exchange for a cap on gains. The long two-year window means buying mid-period leaves different protection than starting at the beginning.
BUFH: A ladder of twelve buffer funds staggered a month apart, each giving large US stocks the maximum available loss protection over its own year. The ladder is the idea: some protection is always freshly in place, so the fund's shield stays steadier than a single annual buffer's.
CGGG: Large US growth companies picked by several Capital Group managers working independently, with technology about half and internet and media names next. The multi-manager style smooths individual stock pickers' swings; it's a classic core growth holding that still rises and falls more than the broad market.
CNBS: US companies in the cannabis and hemp business: growers, dispensaries, cannabis landlords and the pick-and-shovel suppliers around them. It's a focused bet on legal cannabis, a young industry where stocks swing wildly on regulation news and most companies are still small and unprofitable.
DEMZ: Large US companies whose corporate political donations lean Democratic, making it a values-based core holding with a political screen. Technology is nearly half the fund, far more than the broad market, so the donation filter creates a tech-tilted portfolio that can behave quite differently from the whole market.
DHLX: A concentrated set of large US companies the manager believes are priced below their worth, spanning banks, health care, technology and energy. With only a couple of dozen holdings, each judgment counts heavily: the fund can beat the market by a lot when right and lag badly when wrong.
DLFE: Large US stocks in a two-way design over each year starting in February: it can gain when the market rises, up to a cap, and gain when it falls within a buffered range too. The structure targets a positive outcome in flat-to-down years, at the cost of smaller gains in big rallies.
DSTX: Companies outside the US chosen for stable cash flows, clean balance sheets and prices low compared with the cash they generate. It spreads evenly across industries and countries; the cash-flow discipline is the point, avoiding both pricey growth stories and companies with shaky finances.
DVYA: High-dividend companies across the Asia and Pacific region, in Australia, Japan, Hong Kong, Singapore and New Zealand, led by banks and mining giants. It's an income play on the region's mature giants; payouts are the point, and mining and bank shares make it bumpier than US dividend funds.
EVHY: Below-investment-grade corporate bonds, the riskier debt known as junk bonds, picked by an active manager for their higher interest. It plays the high-income role in a portfolio; because its borrowers are weaker, it behaves more like stocks than safer bonds when markets get rough.
FFEM: Emerging market companies picked one by one on business fundamentals by Fidelity managers, leaning heavily toward Asian chip and internet giants. Technology is over two-fifths, so despite the emerging markets label it behaves much like an Asian technology fund with extra political and currency risk.
FFTY: Fifty fast-growing companies from the Investor's Business Daily growth list, chosen for surging earnings and strong price action, refreshed weekly. Health care and technology lead; the list chases momentum, so holdings change fast and the fund can swing sharply when growth stocks fall out of favor.
FLEU: Companies from the countries that use the euro, led by banks at about a quarter, with industrial and technology firms behind them. It's the European counterpart to a US large-cap fund, and because it is not currency hedged, returns for US investors rise and fall with the euro too.
FMCE: Twenty-five to thirty-five US companies chosen as compounders: durable businesses expected to grow their value steadily by reinvesting profits well. Banks and technology firms lead the mix; the short, high-conviction list is the point, so it behaves like a collection of individual stock picks, not the market.
HTAX: Lower-rated municipal bonds, the junk end of the muni market, including Puerto Rico debt, paying interest exempt from federal income tax. Junk munis pay more than high-grade ones, and they fall harder when a big issuer hits trouble, so the tax-free income comes with real credit risk.
JUNM: Large US stocks with the maximum available buffer over each year starting in June, built to absorb as much of any loss as the options allow, in exchange for a low cap on gains. It's the cautious end of the buffer family: maximum protection, minimum excitement, and it will trail stock funds in strong years.
KDEC: Small US companies with a buffer that absorbs part of any loss over each year starting in December, in exchange for a cap on gains. Small caps swing more than big ones, so the cushion is the draw here; in a strong small-cap rally, the cap will hold it back.
LCF: A focused portfolio of large US companies picked by active managers for quality and reasonable prices, with technology and internet giants the largest slice. Focused means roughly a few dozen stocks chosen with conviction: it can beat the market when picks are right and lag when they are not.
LSAT: Mid-sized and larger US companies chosen by a factor model that scores stocks on things like value, quality and momentum, spread across banks, consumer names and technology. It's a focused, actively adjusted portfolio, so the mix can shift as factor scores change rather than staying fixed to an index.
MMKT: A government money market fund holding Treasury bills and similar short-term government instruments, aiming to keep its share price steady at a dollar. It's a place to park cash and earn a little interest, run inside an ETF wrapper rather than a bank account or standard money fund.
MOTI: Companies outside the US with durable competitive advantages, the 'moats' Morningstar analysts rate strongest, bought when their prices look reasonable. It leans toward industrial and consumer brand names in Europe and Japan; the moat focus makes it a quality-tilted overseas core rather than the whole foreign market.
MTGP: Mortgage-backed bonds, mostly government-backed home loans bundled into securities, plus other packaged debt like asset-backed securities and loan bundles. It's an income fund for the bond side of a portfolio, actively managed and using some leverage, so it pays more than plain mortgage funds and moves more too.
MVPA: A concentrated portfolio of twenty to forty companies of any size that the manager believes are worth far more than their prices, led by consumer and financial names. It's high-conviction value investing: patience is required, and the small list means single picks can make or sink the year.
NAUG: The 100 big growth companies of the Nasdaq, technology about three-fifths, combined with a buffer that absorbs part of any loss over each year starting in August, in exchange for a cap on gains. It's a softer way to hold growth stocks, though a strong rally will leave it behind uncapped rivals.
NDOW: A global mix of stock funds, bond funds and alternatives like managed futures and floating-rate loans, assembled by an active manager. It aims for steadier returns with less dependence on US markets alone, accepting smaller gains in strong rallies in exchange for a calmer ride.
NELS: Large US companies mixed with other funds to cover broader ground, actively managed as a select portfolio rather than a full market basket. Technology is about two-fifths; with an active manager choosing the mix, it can drift from the broad market in either direction.
NODE: Companies building the onchain economy: crypto miners, data centers, blockchain platforms and payment firms, plus a slice held directly in a bitcoin fund. It's VanEck's broad take on crypto-linked stocks, so it swings with the digital asset market rather than holding one coin alone.
PBL: Stock market exposure gained through options, cushioned by a large holding of US Treasury bonds, about half the fund. It's designed as ballast for a portfolio: steady in storms and participating in rallies, but its cautious build means it will trail badly in strong bull markets.
PCL: Corporate bonds with more than ten years left until they mature, issued by big banks, phone companies and other large firms. Long-term bonds pay more interest than short ones, but their prices swing the most when interest rates move, so this is the jumpy end of investment-grade bonds.
PZLV: Large US companies bought at deep discounts after falling out of favor, with health care and banks the biggest slices. Pzena's deep value style buys what others have given up on, so the fund can look out of step for years before its bargains pay off, if they do.
RISN: A tactical fund that holds large US stocks while its trend system says the market is rising, and shifts into Treasury bonds and gold when the trend turns down. It's a faith-based manager's take on trend following, aiming to join rallies and sit out slides, though whipsaws can catch it wrong-footed.
RSPE: America's largest companies, screened for environmental, social and governance standards and then weighted equally so each holds roughly the same share. Equal weighting shrinks the mega-cap giants and lifts smaller members, making it less top-heavy than the normal market-weighted version while keeping a similar industry mix.
SHAG: Short-term US investment-grade bonds: Treasuries, government-backed mortgage bonds and corporate debt, arranged to squeeze out a bit more yield than the plain short-term market. It's a low-drama income holding for money that cannot take big swings, though the yield tilt adds a touch more credit risk.
SNOY: Built entirely around Snowflake, the cloud data company, using a synthetic covered call strategy: options create stock-like exposure while sold calls generate monthly income. It's an income play on one volatile tech stock, with gains capped by the calls and losses mostly matching the shares.
SOXY: Chip companies, from designers to equipment makers, held directly, with options sold against them to generate a high stream of income. It's an income-first take on semiconductors: the option premiums smooth the sector's wild swings a little, but they also cap its famous rallies.
SPCT: Established large US companies with strong records of paying and raising dividends, spread evenly across industries from staples to technology. It aims for a calmer core holding built on mature market leaders, trading some growth punch for steadier behavior in rough markets.
TDAX: A leveraged trading fund that aims for 120% to 140% of the daily move of TDAQ, another TappAlpha fund, resetting that boost every day. Daily-reset leverage compounds oddly in choppy markets, so returns over weeks can drift far from the underlying fund's, making it a short-term tool.
TEND: Large US stocks with a targeted shield: over each year starting in December it is built to absorb roughly the first tenth of any loss, in exchange for a cap on gains. The terms reset every December, so the protection left depends on when you buy.
TRUC: Communication services in full: internet platforms, social media, streaming, phone companies and media, held through a sector fund plus individual stocks. The 'true sector' design aims to capture the whole industry as classified today, and with a few giants dominating the sector, it is highly concentrated.
USOY: An income strategy that sells options on an oil fund, turning crude oil price moves into regular cash payments. It's a way to earn income from oil without owning it directly, but gains are capped when oil surges, and it still falls when oil drops hard.
VPX: US stocks chosen and weighted with the business cycle in mind, favoring whichever industries the manager's indicators say fit the current stage. Energy and banks get unusually large shares beside technology; the cycle calls are the point, and mistimed shifts can leave it out of step with the market.
WIMA: Large companies outside the US, mostly banks, industrial firms and drug makers, combined with a moving-average signal that shifts money toward Treasury bills when overseas markets trend down. The adaptive switch is the point: it gives up some upside in choppy markets to try to miss the worst slides.
XDQQ: The Nasdaq's big growth companies with accelerated upside that resets every quarter: gains count at a multiple of the underlying stocks', up to a cap, with no buffer against losses. Technology is about three-fifths, so it is a concentrated, juiced-up growth tool for strong quarters.
XDSQ: Large US stocks with accelerated upside that resets every three months: gains count at a multiple of the market's, up to a cap, each quarter. There's no buffer underneath, so losses land in full; it's a tool for investors expecting a strong quarter, not a protected holding.
XITK: US technology companies in the sector's most innovative corners: chip designers, cloud software, networking and electronic media firms, many of them mid-sized. It's a growth bet beyond the tech giants, spread across smaller innovators, so it swings more than a fund holding only the biggest names.
XJAN: Large US stocks with boosted upside and a moderate cushion: over each year starting in January, gains count at an enhanced rate up to a cap, while a buffer absorbs part of any loss. It's for investors who want more rally participation than a plain buffer fund offers, with less protection.
XYLG: America's largest companies, with call options sold on part of the portfolio to generate income while the rest stays free to grow. It's a middle path between a plain stock fund and a full covered call fund: steadier income than the market, more upside kept than most option-income funds.
YETH: An income strategy on ether, the Ethereum network's cryptocurrency, using options to mimic owning it while selling calls for monthly cash payouts. The calls generate income and cap gains, so it suits investors who want ether exposure that pays, accepting a ceiling on crypto rallies.
ZAPR: America's largest companies with a defined shield over each year starting in April: it is designed to protect against losses across the year, in exchange for a cap on gains. The shield resets every April, so the protection remaining depends on when during the year you buy.
